w: The Predigtstuhl - German for pulpit - rises 1,613m in the Lattengebirge range of the Berchtesgaden Alps, about 2.5km south of Bad Reichenhall. It is one of the few local mountains served by a cable car, long making it a popular tourist attraction, carrying visitors up to panoramic views without the climb.
s: One of the few Berchtesgaden peaks reached by cable car
_facts: 1,613m, Lattengebirge range, ~2.5km south of Bad Reichenhall
One of few local peaks reachable by cable car

w: Hohes Brett - High Plank in German - reaches 2,340m in the Goll massif of the Berchtesgaden Alps, on the Germany-Austria border. Its name refers to the flat, rocky summit plateau, which opens views over the Watzmann's east face, the Hagen Mountains and the Steinernes Meer. Easy to scale, it draws heavy foot traffic.
s: Flat summit plateau facing the Watzmann's east face
_facts: 2,340m, name means 'High Plank' for its flat rocky plateau
Views of the Watzmann's east face, Hagen Mountains and Steinernes Meer

w: Adolf Hitler's holiday home on the Obersalzberg above Berchtesgaden, rebuilt and renamed in 1935. He spent more time here than at any other headquarters through his years in power. RAF bombs damaged it in April 1945, SS troops damaged it further in May, and Allied troops looted it. Bavaria razed the shell in 1952.
_facts: Bombed by the RAF in April 1945, damaged again by SS troops in May, then looted
Burned-out shell demolished by Bavaria in 1952

w: St. Bartholoma stands on the Hirschau peninsula at Konigssee's western shore, reachable only by ship or a long hike. A first chapel here dates to 1134; rebuilt in Baroque style in 1697, modelled on Salzburg Cathedral, with two onion domes and stucco by Joseph Schmidt. An annual pilgrimage still reaches it from Austria.
s: A Baroque pilgrimage church reachable only by boat or hike
_facts: First chapel built 1134; rebuilt in Baroque style in 1697
Modelled on Salzburg Cathedral, stucco by Joseph Schmidt
Reachable only by boat or long hike; annual pilgrimage from Maria Alm, Austria

w: Schonfeldspitze is the second-highest peak in the Steinernes Meer at 2,653m, just behind Selbhorn, on the Austrian side of the Berchtesgaden Alps near the German border. Unusually, its summit cross carries no plain crucifix but a Pieta, Mary cradling the dead Christ, unlike the range's other summit markers.
s: Its summit cross shows a Pieta, not a plain crucifix
_facts: 2,653m, second-highest peak in the Steinernes Meer after Selbhorn
Summit cross depicts a Pieta rather than a plain crucifix

w: The Funtenseetauern rises to 2,579m on the Germany-Austria border, on the northern edge of the Steinernes Meer, its shoulder towering over Konigssee and Obersee below. Climbers approach from the Karlingerhaus, a three-hour route past the Stuhlwand ridge. In winter it is a popular ski tour on the Grosse Reibn route.
s: A border peak towering over Konigssee and Obersee
_facts: 2,579m on the German-Austrian border, overlooks Konigssee and Obersee
Popular winter ski tour, part of the multi-day Grosse Reibn route

w: Christlieger is the only island in Konigssee, near the lake's northern end. Its other name, Johannesinsel, comes from a statue of John of Nepomuk erected there in 1711. Just 61 metres long and up to 26 wide, with a small landing spot for rowing boats; passenger boats to St. Bartholoma cannot dock. Owned by Bavaria.
s: Konigssee's only island, named for an 18th-century statue
_facts: Only island in Konigssee, near the lake's northern end
Named Johannesinsel for a 1711 marble statue of John of Nepomuk
61m by up to 26m; owned by the Free State of Bavaria
